newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE-Bankers join fishermen on Malaysian island.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Bankers join fishermen on Malaysian island.

text.p: The haphazardly built houses in the Patau Patau water village stand on tall stilts over a bay that stinks of rotting fish.

"There's nothing here to see," said 39-year old villager Abdul Rahim. "But you can see the Financial Park from here," he said, pointing to a gleaming complex of glass and steel towers some two kilometres away (1.24 miles).
The Financial Park, housing more than 50 foreign banks and scores of companies, is the new pride of the mostly farming and fishing population of tiny Labuan island.
Located in the South China Sea off the northern coast of Borneo island, the 92-square kilometre (114.26 square mile) island is home to Malaysia's International Offshore Financial centre (IOFC).
OLD PIRATE'S COVE

The government built the 360 million ringgit ($142.8 million) Financial Park to get foreigners to work here. They have begun to trickle in as expensive new homes, golf courses, international schools and medical centres get built.
The lives of Labuan's 60,000 people have not been the same since the IOFC was officially established in October 1990.
The 19th-century pirate's cove is now a tax-haven attracting global financial institutions and luxury yachts in their wake.
Lying halfway between Singapore and Hong Kong in the South China Sea, Labuan aims to compete with them as a regional financial centre.
Moslem Malaysia is especially interested in making Labuan a centre for Islamic-based financial products, such as Islamic banking and insurance, to attract Middle East money.

"The potential is huge to start more Islamic financial instruments and to market them overseas so that we will get world-wide support and not just from Malaysia funds," said Awang Adek Hussin, director-general of the Labuan Offshore Financial Services Authority.
DEPOSITS OF $4.31 BILLION
At the end of last year, deposits of 52 offshore banks based on the island stood at US$4.31 billion, while loans outstanding totalled $11.96 billion.
The government expects 30 insurance companies and related financial service firms to set up by the end of this year.

But while the IOFC now has a critical mass of banks and financial service companies to give it credibility, bankers said it will take awhile before Labuan can rival the likes of the Bahamas and the Cayman Islands.

"We in Labuan can't do it in two, three years," said Lo Nyen Khing, managing director at Citibank Malaysia (Labuan) Ltd. "Singapore took 30 years to build up as a country and regional financial centre -- Hong Kong probably 100 years."
HOUSE RENTALS SHARPLY INCREASED
Labuan's residents and small businessmen complain that the highly paid bankers and their families are driving up the prices of local goods and house rentals have sharply increased.

"My rentals have risen. How can my business improve?" asks Jassa Singh, who sells sporting goods in the town centre. He said his shop rental now costs him 3,400 ringgit a month, about double from 1,800 ringgit in 1990.
Rentals for houses and apartments near the town centre rival that of Malaysia's capital, Kuala Lumpur.
Though bankers regularly fly in and out of the island to make multi-million dollar deals, little of it trickles down to the small businessman.
"This offshore centre is for rich people. It doesn't affect us. If they come here, they stay in the hotels," said Berahim Kurus, a farmer who runs a fruit stall in the town's market.
LUXURY CARS ABOUND
Nowhere, perhaps, is the appearance of big bucks more evident than in the number of luxury cars seen in the small town, including many Mercedes Benzs and top-end Toyota four-wheel drives.
The island's tax-free status means foreign cars are half the price found elsewhere in Malaysia, which has import duties of up to 100 percent or more for imported cars.
"In Labuan, easily 10 Mercedes Benzs are sold a month," said Sebastian Bong, senior sales executive at N.A. Classic Sdn Bhd, a Mercedes distributor on Labuan.
Residents said the island's economy is also supported by Brunei citizens who make the one-hour journey by ferry from the Borneo coast.
BRUNEI TOURISTS

"The seminar people (of the Financial Park) sometimes come over. But Brunei people come here on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays," said clothes-seller Anna, who helps run a small stall in the town's market.
With one Brunei dollar worth roughly 1.75 ringgit, the Bruneians also come over for the cheaper seafood and entertainment.
More Malaysians would visit Labuan if airfares to Peninsular Malaysia were reduced and more tourist attractions added, residents said.
"Our rooms are full when there are big conferences. Otherwise, they're only 30, 40 percent full," said a front-desk officer at the Sheraton Labuan.
But to people at the water village, the luxury cars, the bankers and the seminars are so near and yet so far.
Said villager Abdul Rahim: "We have better jobs. But I can't afford to buy a new house as prices have jumped."
($1 = 2.52 ringgit)
